cards.title: Why your ad creative—not your targeting—selects the buyer
cards.summary: Meta's system replaced interest/lookalike labels with vector-based targeting, so audience selection now happens through your creative and the algorithm's clustering.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate budget between targeting settings and creative production, or when an agency proposes rebuilding interest and lookalike ad sets.
steps: Accept the source's frame: as of the 2023–2026 rebuild, Meta selects the audience, not your manually entered interests. The practical implication is that creative is the lever you control for audience selection.

Understand the mechanism to reason about your account: instead of a static 'pets' label, Meta plots each user as a vector in a very high-dimensional space and nudges that vector with every organic and paid interaction, so users cluster by behavior rather than by declared interest.
When you run broad targeting, treat early spend as a probe: Meta spreads impressions across the space, observes who engages and buys, then concentrates delivery on the clusters that converted.

Because of that mechanism, ask what your creative visually and verbally signals, since the algorithm reads the ad to find the matching cluster. Distinct concepts reach distinct clusters; near-identical ads reach the same one.

Deprecate dependence on interest and lookalike targeting in your structure. The source states interests/lookalikes were deprecated in July 2025 and says broad targeting outperforms interest targeting on large data sets over long periods.
Keep the controls the source says you still hold: exclusions, minimum age, locations (never worldwide by default), and languages.
caveats: The 'broad always beats interests' claim is the presenter's position, tied to large data sets and long time horizons, not a guaranteed result for small budgets or narrow catalogs.
Age bands and gender are only treated as suggestions, not controls, per the source.

cards.title: The three-stage Meta delivery pipeline: retrieval, ranking, auction
cards.summary: Every impression passes through retrieval (Andromeda shortlisting from tens of millions of ads), ranking (relevance scoring), then the auction, all in roughly 200 milliseconds.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why ads get no delivery or poor performance, or deciding whether a change targets creative, structure, or bid.
steps: Map your problem to the stage it belongs to. Retrieval is where Meta scans the full ad inventory and shortlists a few thousand candidates relevant to the user. If your ads are never retrieved, creative signal and account structure are the suspects.
Ranking is where shortlisted ads are scored for relevance and personal fit, using the user's historical paid and organic interactions. Creative diversity and offer clarity drive this stage.
The auction is the final stage, where hundreds of ads bid for the placement. Bid and economics live here.
When Meta ships an update, identify which stage it touches (retrieval, ranking, or auction dynamics) so you adapt the corresponding part of your account instead of rewriting everything.

Useful update history for orientation: Lattice (2023) consolidated ranking, a November 2024 sequence-learning update optimized across ad sequences (supporting one ad per ad set structures), Andromeda (December 2024) changed retrieval via creative understanding, GEM added multimodal reading of video/audio and grouping by format, and an adaptive ranking model allocates compute per impression.
Do not expect platform updates to lift your ROAS; the source's expectation is that your ROAS holds roughly flat while Meta raises CPMs to capture the efficiency gains.
caveats: The 200-millisecond figure and 3% conversion / 5% CTR platform-lift claims come from Meta and the presenter flags platform number claims as things to treat carefully.
Update names and dates are historical context; verify current behavior against Meta's own documentation, which the presenter says he is sourcing.

cards.title: Trigger creative fatigue deliberately, then refresh before ROAS tapers
cards.summary: Very specific persona-callout ads saturate their cluster fast, after which Meta either re-serves the same people or drifts outside your ICP and ROAS declines.
cards.use_when: Planning creative refresh cadence, or explaining declining ROAS and rising frequency on a narrowly targeted persona-based ad.
steps: Recognize the mechanism: a highly specific ad (for example, a callout to business owners doing $10M+/year) causes Meta to converge on that narrow cluster and saturate it.
Expect the source's reported pattern: saturation can arrive around $10,000 in spend on such a narrow concept, after which there is no one new in the cluster to reach.

When saturation hits, Meta either keeps showing the ad to the same users (frequency climbs) or expands outward to adjacent clusters who are no longer your ideal customer profile, which is why ROAS tapers as the algorithm bridges out.

Pre-empt this by maintaining a pipeline of diverse concepts rather than repeatedly iterating one persona. Iterations are fine inside the account, but reaching net-new audiences requires diversity in concepting.
Define concepts as the intersection of an angle, an offer, and a persona. Changing format may also register as a different ad with Meta even when angle, offer, and persona stay constant.
Monitor frequency and cluster-level spend as your refresh triggers rather than waiting for ROAS to visibly decay.
caveats: The ~$10K saturation point is an illustrative example from the presenter's experience, not a benchmark to plan budgets against.
This describes behavior the presenter attributes to the algorithm; treat it as a model for decision-making, not a documented rule.

cards.title: Use exclusions to stop budget leaking to your warm customer cluster
cards.summary: Meta preferentially serves ads to warm clusters already likely to convert, so if you don't exclude existing customers, the algorithm will spend on people who would have bought anyway.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new broad-targeting campaign or auditing whether reported conversion efficiency is inflated by existing customers.
steps: Understand the risk: because vector clusters can correspond to warm existing customers, Meta is incentivized to push your ads there since conversion likelihood is high. This can mask poor new-customer acquisition.
Build exclusion audiences for existing customers and apply them to your acquisition campaigns, so delivery is forced toward net-new clusters rather than the warm core.
Treat exclusions as the single most important targeting control you still own, since interests, lookalikes, and other manual targeting have been deprecated or reduced to suggestions.
Pair exclusions with the other retained controls: minimum age (a real control, unlike age bands, which are only suggestions), locations (don't default to worldwide), and languages.
When reviewing performance, separate existing-customer conversions from new-customer conversions so you can tell whether the algorithm is prospecting or harvesting.
If you also run retargeting, keep it deliberate and separated from acquisition so the two aren't bidding for the same warm cluster unintentionally.
caveats: The source presents this as a growing risk under vector-based delivery; the magnitude depends on your customer file quality and how well your exclusions are matched.
Exclusions reduce reachable audience, which is intentional but means your addressable pool shrinks as your customer base grows.

cards.title: Bid equation: relevance multipliers beat raising bids
cards.summary: Placement goes to Bid × Estimated Action Rate + Ad Quality, so a lower bidder with superior relevance can beat you—being more relevant is the faster route to cheaper delivery.
cards.use_when: Considering whether to raise bids to win more auctions, or diagnosing why a competitor wins placements at a lower apparent cost.
steps: Internalize the formula: winning the auction equals bid times estimated action rate, plus ad quality.
Note that estimated action rate is expected CTR times expected conversion rate, so both click and post-click behavior feed the multiplier.

Use the practical consequence: two advertisers showing the same product to the same person can win at very different bids, so a $1 bid can lose to a $0.50 bid if the cheaper advertiser's relevance and quality are superior.
Therefore treat 'be more relevant' as the primary cost-reduction lever rather than increasing bids, which just buys placement at worse unit economics.

Do not chase ad quality directly. The source says quality score is not visible and changes in every auction, and attempts to optimize it directly are likened to star signs. Do the fundamentals and accept that it is immeasurable.
Treat estimated action rate and ad quality as diagnostic (rearview) metrics, not live levers you can tune inside the auction.

The presenter's strongest claim: economics are the real bid—higher sustainable bid from better AOV, LTV, and gross margin wins more auctions and scales further than platform tactics. The source asserts you cannot out-tactic bad economics.
caveats: The claim that better economics dominate creatives, structure, and measurement is the presenter's opinion; it is directionally useful but not a universal law.
Quality score optimization advice is explicitly called unreliable by the source because the metric is not measurable by advertisers.

cards.title: Turn estimated action rate into a CPM arbitrage through landing-page action design
cards.summary: The source reports that high-action landing experiences correlate with far lower CPMs, suggesting you can design for a high action rate to reduce what you pay for delivery.
cards.use_when: Designing or comparing landing pages, lead capture, or checkout flows where you want to lower effective ad costs.
steps: Consider the source's non-ecommerce illustration as a model: a lead-magnet funnel with 30–70% landing-page conversion reportedly saw CPMs around $25, while a book-a-call funnel with 3–6% landing-page conversion reportedly saw CPMs around $100—same lead event triggered in both.
Extract the mechanism without copying the funnel: when a high proportion of users complete the on-page action, Meta appears to read strong action rate and reduce CPMs; when few do, it charges more.

Apply this to ecommerce by increasing the proportion of visitors who complete a meaningful event on your landing or product page—clear offers, obvious next action, low friction—rather than only optimizing the ad.
Test whether the effect shows up in your own account by comparing CPMs across landing pages or offer types that trigger the same conversion event.
Be aware the presenter cannot fully prove why Meta prices this way (whether via expected action rate alone or also reading page value), so treat this as a hypothesis to test rather than a certainty.
If it holds in your data, deliberately choose funnel and page structures that maximize completed actions on the page to find cost arbitrage.
caveats: The $25 vs $100 CPM figures are the presenter's observations from service funnels, explicitly outside ecommerce. Do not treat them as ecommerce benchmarks.
The causal explanation is the presenter's own hypothesis and he acknowledges it is hard to prove; validate on your own account before rearchitecting funnels.

cards.title: Improve Event Match Quality to feed an accurate action rate
cards.summary: If Meta only sees a fraction of your conversions, it computes a lower estimated action rate than reality, eroding your auction position—so signal quality is a real if small lever.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing pixel/CAPI tracking, or when reported conversions clearly undercount actual sales.
steps: Run the arithmetic to see the exposure: if ads drive 100 conversions but Meta tracks only 70, Meta computes action rate from those 70. If the true conversion rate is 3% but Meta sees 2%, the bidding equation is working from a depressed number.
Because estimated action rate feeds the auction, underreported conversions mean you lose auctions you should win—not because your ads are worse, but because Meta's view of them is.
Improve signal quality by ensuring conversions flow back through the pixel and Conversions API (CAPI) so Event Match Quality (EMQ) is high and clean.
Prioritize this on the events that matter for your objective (purchase, lead, add-to-cart) rather than trying to perfect every event.

Set expectations honestly: the source treats server-side tracking as a 'nice to have.' If it fits on the P&L, add it on the assumption it probably helps, but do not budget for a visible efficiency jump.

The presenter says he has tried to measure server-side tracking's impact multiple times and found it too small against week-to-week noise to reach statistical confidence—so do not run a before/after test expecting a clean read.
caveats: Server-side tracking is heavily marketed; the source explicitly warns that its measurable impact is very hard to establish and results may not change visibly.
EMQ and CAPI interfaces change—verify current setup and configuration requirements in Meta's current documentation before implementing.

cards.title: Avoid the Entity ID trap by engineering true concept diversity
cards.summary: Meta groups near-identical ads under one Entity ID, so 200 similar ads can register as ~20 unique entities and serve the same audience pool, wasting the rest of your volume.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a creative library, or when adding many ad variations has produced no incremental reach or conversion lift.
steps: Recognize the failure mode: Andromeda scans your ads, identifies duplicates, and groups them under a single Entity ID. The source's example is 200 uploaded ads registering as only about 20 unique ads, grouped in batches of roughly ten.
Understand why this is costly: grouped ads serve the same audience cluster, which yields no unique reach across the group and does not raise purchase likelihood through repetition.
Restate the goal: the point of adding concepts is to reach more unique people or convert existing people. Serving near-duplicates to the same pool achieves neither.
Diagnose before producing more assets: ask how many genuinely distinct concepts (angle × offer × persona) exist in the account, not how many files were uploaded.

Increase diversity at the concept level. The source notes that changing format substantially can also register as a different ad even with the same angle, offer, and persona—useful when you want more registered entities without inventing new angles.
Keep iterations, but do not count them as diversity. Iterations do not reach net-new clusters; only distinct concepts do.
caveats: The 200-ads-to-20-entities ratio is an illustrative example, not a fixed grouping threshold.
You cannot see entity grouping directly in the ad account, so this must be reasoned about through concept planning rather than observed as a metric.

cards.title: Use the 20% budget-increase rule correction: it's a lag effect, not a learning reset
cards.summary: The common advice not to raise budgets more than 20% has no Meta documentation behind it; apparent post-increase dips are delayed purchases from newly reached audiences.
cards.use_when: Planning budget scaling on a winning campaign, or interpreting a revenue dip immediately after a budget increase.
steps: Do not organize scaling around the 20% cap as if it were algorithm law. The source states there is no Meta documentation for it and that raising budgets by more than 20% is routinely fine.
Explain the dip with the right mechanism: rapid budget increases reach new audiences who need time to see multiple ads before purchasing, so revenue does not scale on the same day.
Consequently do not judge a big budget increase by same-day or next-day revenue. Evaluate over a window long enough for the lag effect to resolve.
The presenter attributes the persistent belief to misreading this business lag as an algorithm reset.
When planning a significant increase, model it as a step change in audience exposure with a delayed conversion tail, and set expectations with stakeholders accordingly.
Pair budget increases with creative diversity so the additional spend has genuinely new clusters to reach rather than re-serving saturated ones.
caveats: This directly contradicts widely repeated advice; the source's position is that the rule is undocumented folklore, but the underlying time-to-purchase lag is real and must still be planned for.
No specific budget-increase percentage is recommended by the source—only that the 20% cap is not a documented constraint.

cards.title: Consolidate account structure to unify conversion data—but keep justified segmentation
cards.summary: Campaign and ad set structure exists to signal segmentation to the algorithm; over-splitting silos learning data, while consolidation pools it and tends to perform better across platforms.
cards.use_when: Auditing campaign/ad set/ad structure, or deciding whether two product lines or sub-brands should share a campaign.
steps: Ask the source's framing question: why does the campaign → ad set → ad hierarchy exist at all, rather than dumping all ads into one account? It exists because platforms need a manual signal that certain ads should learn separately.

Recognize the cost of over-segmentation: campaigns and ad sets do not share data; each learns in isolation. Hyper-segmented structures with many campaigns, many ad sets, and few ads each split conversion data and produce worse performance—on Meta, Google, and TikTok alike.
Default toward consolidation, especially at low spend, because pooling conversion data gives the machine learning more to work with.

Carve out segmentation only where the audience genuinely differs. The source's example is an ice-bath line and a sauna line within one website, which resonate with different people and may warrant separate learning.
Use the same test for any split: are these ads different enough that they should not share data? If not, consolidate.

Combine consolidation with recent algorithm behavior: the November 2024 sequence-learning update means the platform optimizes across sequences of ads to a user, which the source says requires structuring accounts accordingly (one ad per ad set).
caveats: Consolidation is not an absolute rule—the source explicitly allows segmentation for genuinely distinct audiences.
The 'one ad per ad set' structure is tied by the source to the November 2024 update; verify current recommended structures against Meta's current guidance.

cards.title: Treat unit economics as the scaling constraint, not platform tactics
cards.summary: Sustained scaling comes from higher AOV, LTV, and gross margin that fund higher sustainable bids; competitors with better economics can outbid you despite worse creative and structure.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition budget ceilings, prioritizing between creative testing and offer/margin improvements, or diagnosing a ceiling on scale.
steps: Reframe the bid as economics: your bid reflects what your business can sustainably pay, so more margin available for acquisition means more auctions won and more scale achieved.
List the economic inputs that determine your ceiling—pricing, cost of goods, average order value, gross profit per order, LTV, and units per transaction / average unit retail on first order.
Accept the source's blunt claim: a competitor with better unit economics can have worse creatives, worse structure, and worse measurement and still outperform you by simply bidding more.

Therefore prioritize raising gross profit on first purchase—post-purchase upsells, bundles, or a stronger offer—over micro-optimizations like signal tweaks, which the source says deliver far less leverage.

Review 365-day LTV payback, not just first-order economics, when deciding how aggressively you can bid, because the source frames winning at scale as requiring both the economics and the retention game.
Sequence your work accordingly: the presenter says audits should start at the economics level, because if the finance doesn't work you cannot win these platforms regardless of tactics.
caveats: This is the presenter's strategic position ('you cannot out-tactic bad economics'); it is a prioritization argument, not a guarantee that economics alone determines outcomes.
The source notes the presenter's agency has run this approach for ecommerce and retail brands; treat that as context, not proof of results.

cards.title: Stop optimizing for relevance and quality directly—diversify instead
cards.summary: Ad quality and expected action rate are per-user diagnostics computed after the fact, so the actionable proxy is broader asset diversity that is relevant to more people.
cards.use_when: When a stakeholder asks you to 'improve ad relevance/quality score,' or when deciding how to invest creative effort.
steps: Recognize the conceptual error: relevance is determined per user in each individual auction, so trying to optimize a single account-level relevance number is not actionable.
Treat estimated action rate and ad quality as diagnostics—rearview indicators of past CTR and conversion behavior—not inputs you can set.
Redirect the effort: build better diversity across assets so your library is relevant to a wider pool of people, which is what actually feeds the metrics that matter.

In practice, this means producing distinct concepts (angle × offer × persona) rather than many cosmetic variants, and accepting that a single ad's relevance to a given user cannot be engineered directly.
Use these diagnostics retrospectively: if action rate or quality indicators are weak, look for a diversity or offer/landing problem rather than searching for a settings tweak.
Remember that quality score itself is not visible to advertisers and changes in every auction, so no dashboard will confirm improvement.
caveats: The presenter concedes there are genuine fundamentals worth doing—he objects to advanced tinkering aimed at a metric you cannot measure.
This contradicts a large body of popular advice that treats ad relevance as an optimizable lever; the source positions that advice as misreading diagnostics as inputs.

cards.title: Prune deprecated targeting advice from your Meta playbook
cards.summary: Several widely repeated Meta tactics are outdated or undocumented—interests/lookalikes, cookie deprecation warnings, Lattice education, and the 20% budget rule—so audit inherited advice before acting on it.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an agency proposal, onboarding a new media buyer, or refreshing internal SOPs for Meta campaigns.
steps: Interest and lookalike targeting: the source states these were deprecated in July 2025. Stop building structure around them.
Lattice: it is a 2023 update, not a current change. Education built around 'the new Lattice update' is stale.
Cookies: the source says Chrome kept cookies, with the decision made in April 2025. Advice premised on cookie deprecation is not a current constraint.
The 20% budget-increase rule: no Meta documentation supports it, per the source. Do not plan scaling around it.
Direct quality-score optimization: not measurable, so treat specific tactics for raising it with skepticism.

Build a review habit: when you encounter a Meta tactic, ask which stage of retrieval, ranking, or auction it claims to affect, and whether it is documented. This filters inherited folklore from mechanics that matter.
Keep the controls that remain real: exclusions, minimum age, location, language, plus consolidation, concept diversity, signal quality, and economics.
caveats: These are the presenter's corrections as stated in the source; platform behavior changes, so verify against Meta's current documentation before removing anything from a live account.
Cookie and targeting policy changes are the kind of facts most likely to have moved since the source was recorded.

Understanding that Estimated Action Rate and Ad Quality are diagnostic metrics (rearview indicators) and that true scaling requires feeding diverse creative concepts to the algorithm to map to net-new audience clusters.
